data_profile.ambiguity_note: Several class boundaries are inherently ambiguous in H&E histopathology: 'debris' vs 'background' vs 'mucus' overlap in appearance; 'cancer-associated stroma' vs 'smooth muscle' can be indistinguishable at the patch level; 'normal colon mucosa' vs early 'colorectal adenocarcinoma epithelium' involves a dysplastic continuum. The test set (CRC-VAL-7K) originates from a different clinical center, introducing uncontrolled variation in staining protocol, scanner calibration, and tissue preparation that can shift the visual appearance of every class, compounding label ambiguity. The test prevalence,
ambiguity_risks: Cross-institutional domain shift: test images from a different clinical center introduce uncontrolled staining, scanner, and tissue-preparation variability that is not captured by train/val splits.

Severe class-prevalence shift in test: 'adipose' prevalence nearly doubles (10.4%→18.6%, ratio 1.79) while 'debris' nearly halves (11.5%→4.7%, ratio 0.41), violating the i.i.d. assumption and biasing accuracy metrics.
Small per-class test counts (debris n=339, stroma n=421, smooth muscle n=592) yield high variance in per-class accuracy and make confidence intervals wide.
Label ambiguity between 'debris', 'background', and 'mucus' is exacerbated by inter-center staining differences, increasing misclassification risk that is not a model failure but a definitional one.
'Cancer-associated stroma' vs 'smooth muscle' boundary is patch-level ambiguous; inter-center variation in section thickness and fixation can shift which label a pathologist assigns.
Test-to-train prevalence ratios span 0.41–1.79, meaning a model trained on the train distribution will face a shifted prior at test time, inflating apparent error for under-represented test classes.
The 1.63× train imbalance is mild, but the effective test imbalance (adipose:debris ≈ 4:1) is substantially higher, so overall accuracy in the test set is dominated by adipose and mucus predictions.

No information on whether the 9-class taxonomy was applied identically across centers; a single pathologist vs. multi-reader labeling protocol difference would introduce systematic label noise in the test set.
